subtopic: FULFILMENT OF OBLIGATIONS AND PURPOSES OF COVENANT, ESPECIALLY AS TO SANCTIONS AND THE CAUSES OF WAR
speechtext:
The desire for peace is
not a monopoly of any party in this house. I believe it is true that the great majority of members of this house, as well as the great majority of the people of Canada, are in favour of peace. During the last year a most
remarkable thing has taken place in Great Britain. The result of a peace ballot, taken under the direction of Lord Cecil, one of the great crusaders for peace, and in which almost thirteen million ballots were returned, shows the following facts:
In answer to the question: should Great Britain remain a member of the League of Nations, 97 per cent answered "yes" in relation to those who answered "no."
In answer to the question: are you in favour of an all round reduction of armaments by national agreement, 92-5 per cent answered "yes" in relation to those who answered "no."
In answer to the question: are you in favour of an all round abolition of national military and naval aircraft by international agreement, 85 per cent answered "yes" in relation to those who answered "no."
In answer to the question: should the manufacture and sale of arms for private profit be prohibited by national agreement, 93-1 per cent answered "yes" in relation to those who answered "no."
In answer to the question: do you consider that if one nation insists on attacking another, the other nations should combine to compel it to stop by economic and non-military means, 94-1 per cent answered "yes" in relation to those who answered "no."
To the last question: do you consider that if a nation insists on attacking another, the other nations should combine to compel it to stop, by if necessary, military measures, 74-2 per cent answered "yes" in relation to those who answered "no."
We have no statistics of a similar nature in Canada. But the resolutions passed by several national bodies and by church organizations, and the general sentiments expressed in the press, would lead one to believe that, like the motherland, the great majority of the Canadian people are opposed to war and are in favour of taking whatever steps are necessary to maintain peace.
I draw these facts to the attention of the house because I want to make it clear that we in this corner are not presenting this resolution with the self-righteous attitude that we are the sole champions of peace. I think we all want peace. The question is, how can we 'best maintain peace? It is not a question of peace or war. It is a question of what is the best policy that shall make for peace for the prevention of war. A year ago this was a very simple question to answer. To-day it is not quite so simple. The whole confusing subject of sanctions has arisen. Certain events of the last year have confused the minds of those who desire peace, with the

League of Nations-Mr. Douglas
result that the ranks of peace lovers have become somewhat disorganized and it is necessary now to think the whole question over again.
May I in leading up to the subject review very briefly what has occurred since the beginning of what is called the Italo-Ethiopian question. The whole dispute began as a result of a border incident known as the Walwal incident, which took place on November 23, 1934. Subsequently a commission was set up to investigate the matter, and it finally decided that neither nation was to blame. From January, 1935, until last July, friction increased rather than decreased. The Italian government continued to pour troops and munitions into Africa, apparently with a view to military aggression. The major powers of Europe who were concerned endeavoured- I think unfortunately-to settle this matter outside of the machinery of the league; that is, their negotiations were based entirely on the Tripartite Agreement of 1906 and the revision treaties of 1926 and 1928. There was no recourse to the machinery of the league during the whole of the time that the Italian government was massing troops in Africa. It was not until July last that the major powers referred the case of Italy and Ethiopia to the League of Nations. I think we may be proud of the fact that on that occasion the lead was given by Right Hon. Sir Samuel Hoare, then British Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs. At that time, in a brilliant and spirited defence of the League of Nations, Sir Samuel Hoare placed the British government and the British people solidly behind collective action to maintain collective peace. I shall read just the closing part of that address:
In conformity with its precise and explicit obligations, the league stands, and my country stands with it, for the collective maintenance of the covenant in its entirety, and particularly for steady and collective resistance to all acts of unprovoked aggression. The attitude of the British nation in the last few weeks has clearly demonstrated the fact that this is no variable and unreliable sentiment, but a principle of international conduct to which they and their government hold with firm, enduring and universal persistance.
I say, I think we may well be proud of the fact that a British foreign minister, backed by the peace ballot to which I have referred and by the growing sentiment in Great Britain that the British people were prepared to make tremendous sacrifices in order to maintain collective peace, placed the British people solidly behind the League of Nations on that occasion. I should like to point out also that on that occasion Canada as well was placed

solidly behind the League of Nations. I quote the closing paragraph of the speech delivered by Hon. Howard Ferguson on September 14, 1935:
Impressed, then, by the gravity of the situation, my government has requested me to make its position clear with regard to this matter. Canada believes the league of nations is an indispensable agency for world peace. We cannot agree that any member is warranted in resorting to war to enforce its claims in violation of its solemn pledges to seek and find a peaceful settlement of every dispute. We hope that an honourable and peaceful solution of the Ethiopian controversy will yet be reached. If, unfortunately, this proves not to be the case, Canada will join with the other members of the league in considering how, by unanimous action, peace can be maintained.
Thus in July last the machinery of the League of Nations was invoked as a means of settling what had become a very critical question. Ten years ago, when the league was being discussed somewhat critically, there were those who said it was so weighty that it would be simply impossible to get it to function quickly in a time of crisis. I am sure, however, that even the most optimistic supporters of the league hardly believed that the league would actually function as quickly as it really did. I have little doubt that the period from October 7 to October 14 will go down in history as a most remarkable phenomenon of international collective action. You will remember, sir, that hostilities were begun on October 4, and this is actually what happened in the following few days. On Monday, October 7, thirteen members of the council of the League of Nations found Italy guilty of resorting to war in disregard of her covenants. On Wednesday, October 9, the verdict of the council was referred to the assembly of the League of Nations, consisting of fifty-four nations. On Thursday, October 10, this verdict was passed upon by the assembly of the league, which found Italy guilty; fifty-one nations, representing four-fifths of the population of the earth, concurred in that decision; five nations were absent and three nations voted against the verdict. On Friday, the 11th, the committee on sanctions formally approved an embargo on arms to Italy and the removal of restrictions against Ethiopia, and on Saturday, October 12, financial experts proposed credit restrictions against Italy and Mr. Anthony Eden proposed a boycott on the import of Italian periodicals. Thus in this short period from October 7 to October 14 the league-though somewhat late, I think-swung into action and took the necessary steps, first of all to condemn the aggressor and second to set machinery in motion to prevent that aggressor receiving

League of Nations-Mr. Douglas
the necessary materials with which to carry on war.
In order to keep the logic of our sequence intact let us look for a moment at what was done by the Canadian government at this time. Hon. Howard Ferguson, undoubtedly under orders from the government of Canada, -the previous administration,-made this statement on October 11:
The sole problem before the committee was to decide what sanctions the delegations could all agree upon that afternoon and put into application immediately. Let them show the world that the league was no longer to be scoffed or laughed at, but that it meant business, and that when a breach of its covenant took place it proposed to deal with the aggressor in the proper way. Otherwise the league and the assembly would lose prestige and influence in the world and might as well be dissolved. If the delegates were not at Geneva to see that the covenant was carried out, there was no purpose in their being there at all.
This was followed, on October 29, by a statement from the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), who said:
The government has no doubt it expresses the overwhelmingly conviction of the people of Canada in declaring its continued and firm adherence to the fundamental aims and ideals of the league of nations, and its intention to make participation in the league the cornerstone of its foreign policy in the general field.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that the government of Canada, both the previous administration and the present government, interpreted correctly the psychological attitude of the Canadian people, in that they desired in the main a firm adherence to the policies of the League of Nations and were prepared to take any reasonable steps to preserve peace and prevent a recurrence of war.
There is no need for me to do more than touch very briefly on the sanctions that were suggested and proposed by the coordinating committee. They were five in number: First, an embargo on arms, munitions and implements of war; second, a restriction on loans and credits to Italy; third, a restriction on imports from Italy consisting mainly of periodicals, magazines and papers; fourth, an embargo on key products used by Italy to carry on war, and fifth, mutual economic support given to nations participating in this economic boycott. Canada agreed with all five, the last one in principle and the other four in their entirety.
I have given, sir, this brief review of what has happened during the last year, so that we might understand more clearly just what the problem is that confronts us at the present time. No doubt many people who desire peace are asking themselves if it is wise to
apply sanctions, if it is wise to extend these sanctions, and exactly what the policy of those who desire peace ought to be. There are those, quite sincere people, who take the attitude that we ought to remain neutral, to isolate ourselves; they agree with the great body of public opinion in the republic to the south, that we should cut ourselves adrift from the League of Nations and from European diplomacy. To that argument it may be said, first, that such an attitude is scarcely morally justifiable. I need only quote a statement of Lord Cecil, who said:
Loyalty to this principle of "pooled security" is as necessary to the great society of nations as it is to the society of citizens within the nations. We have to "respect" the broad rules of peace ourselves; but we must also "preserve" them against violence, as the covenant affirms. Every isolationist who challenges this principle and who says in effect "am I my brother's keeper?" is a contributor to anarchy: he is keeping alive the anarchic conception of "security" as meaning a precarious "supremacy" in a world of competing armament, and is preventing the emergence of a new, rational conception of "security" as meaning the public assurance of solidarity against violence and wrong.
Then, Mr. Speaker, even if a policy of isolation were not morally unjustifiable, practically it is not feasible. The one nation in all the world which might have remained neutral in a time of war was the United States of America, a self-sustaining nation which in 1914 decided that she would have no part in the war, and in 1917 elected President Wilson on the platform that he would keep the United States out of the war; but five months later she was plunged into the conflict. In a time of war an exporting nation must send out its ships unless it is to succumb to economic stagnation. If its ships sail the seas they are likely to be attacked or sunk, international complications set in, and the policy of isolation becomes next to impossible.
There are those who maintain to-day that if we invoke economic sanctions they will lead to military sanctions, and that economic sanctions will lead to war. May I point out, first, what sometimes we do not recognize, that failure to apply economic sanctions may lead to war. The League of Nations cannot stand the loss of prestige that would result from permitting the Italo-Ethiopian dispute to go on without intervention. The Sino-Japanese affair caused the prestige of the League of Nations to suffer greatly. If the league again suffers a diplomatic defeat the only remaining agency for international peace will be completely dismembered. I am not one of those who give unswerving allegiance to the League of Nations; I believe it has its
League of Nations-Mr. Douglas

shortcomings, and that it has been used again and again to pull the chestnuts out of the fire for certain imperial interests. But I maintain that it is the only available agency to-day for collective action and collective security. Those who say that if we invoke economic sanctions it will lead to military sanctions forget that if all the fifty-two nations which have promised to invoke those sanctions cooperate, military sanctions will become unnecessary. No nation, no matter how great, could long stand the pressure of an economic boycott on the part of fifty-two other nations. But may I point out that economic sanctions do not necessarily mean military sanctions. I have not time to read article 16 of the covenant of the league, but most hon. members know that in that article economic sanctions are absolute; military sanctions are conditional. It will be remembered, too, that in 1920 Canada made a reservation to article 16. This is it:
It is in conformity with the spirit of article 10 that, in the event of the council considering it to be its duty to recommend the application of military measures in consequence of aggression or danger or threat of aggression, the council shall be bound to take into account, more particularly, the geographical situation and especial condition of each state.
May I remind hon. members that in 1921 the League of Nations in sending a note to Germany made it quite clear that military sanctions would not be compulsory, but were dependent entirely on the regional and geographical situation of the nations. Therefore the argument that the application of economic sanctions must lead to the application of military sanctions and thus to war is not well founded.
In the resolution which I have the honour to present to the house we are asking for a more sincere fulfilment of our obligations under the covenant of the league. We believe that can be done in two ways: first by tightening up the present sanctions, that is by extending the list of things that shall be prohibited from export to include all articles necessary to carry on war. I have no wish to bring up what is sometimes called the Riddell incident; it has been discussed in a more or less partisan way, and we are dealing just now with something that rises above party politics. But I would remind the house that when we are talking about collective action someone has to initiate that action; that when the members of the League of Nations gather to decide what steps they shall take for the maintenence of peace, somebody must propose the steps that should be taken. I submit that there is perhaps no nation represented at the council table of the league that is in

a better position to initiate such steps than Canada. By asking for a more sincere application we mean not only an extension of the list of articles now under embargo but also a tightening up, with a view to investigating what commodities are being shipped indirectly to countries engaged in active aggression. I have the figures here for the export of nickel. It is a remarkable thing that last year, 1935, we exported more nickel than in any year of the last ten. That some of this nickel is being used indirectly to provide armaments for war is almost beyond question. I know it is very difficult to deal with the question of indirect exports. I know there arises the question of remuneration of those who stand to lose by such an arrangement. Yet I submit that the great majority of the Canadian people would support any steps the government might take to see that goods produced in Canada are not being used to enable one nation to carry on a brutal and ruthless massacre of a primitive and defenceless people.
In the resolution I have presented we point out that sanctions are not in themselves sufficient. We point out the danger and futility of sanctions. In the first instance they are dangerous because they may 'be used for the advancement of imperialism. There are those to-day who are pointing with a critical finger to the fact that Great Britain, who was so active in applying sanctions against Italy, was loth to apply them against Japan. They say the reason is that there is a Suez canal in Africa, but no Suez in Manchuria. I am not one who holds that point of view. However, there is a decided danger that sanctions with a view to maintaining peace may be used to maintain and advance imperialistic means of aggrandizement.
There is a danger of sanctions being used to maintain the status quo. I believe President Wilson was the man who, perhaps more than anyone else, was responsible for the drawing up of the covenant of the league. He saw the danger that the league, which was to be an instrument of justice, might become an instrument of injustice, and that as the years went by certain international problems might crop up and necessarily international readjustments would have to be made. He saw that from time to time there would have to be a rearrangement of treaties, particularly a revision of the treaty of Versailles, and that it would be necessary to set up the machinery whereby that revision could take place. For these reasons we point out that in themselves sanctions may constitute a danger, and not only may they be dangerous but they may be futile in the prevention of war. To-day sanctions may postpone war; they may pre-

League of Nations-Mr. Dowlas
vent its happening in the immediate future, but unless the League of Nations is prepared to deal with the underlying causes 'leading to war we cannot hope to maintain peace. Unless we are prepared to see that there are economic problems, that there are colonial problems, that there is a pressure of population in certain areas of the world which inevitably must lead to war, and unless we set up the machinery necessary for peaceable change, the mere application of sanctions will only postpone the inevitable day of reckoning. That is why we have made these proposals.
As I have not much more time to speak I shall not deal in detail with the proposals, but we ask that first of all Canada shall take the lead in securing collective reduction of armaments. If we are going to condemn Italy for breaking article 10 of the covenant, and Germany for breaking the treaty of Versailles, we must be prepared to observe article 8 by which we promise to reduce armaments. There must be collective and open diplomacy, and an abrogation of treaties not in accord with the covenant. Above all, under article 19 we must set up the machinery whereby the problems of territorial expansion, pressure of population, and economic stagnation and suffocation shall be submitted to some body with authority which will be in a position to suggest possible ways of peaceable change.
Change is coming; it is bound to come. The only sensible procedure would seem to be that of setting up the machinery whereby it may be done peaceably and without recourse to force. Unless we recognize this fact, all our talk about sanctions is beside the point. The founder of the league and Right Hon. Sir Samuel Hoare, Lord Lothian and a number of other prominent men who have worked tirelessly for peace, have made this point dear.
I suggest further that we do away with unilateral agreements.

subtopic: FULFILMENT OF OBLIGATIONS AND PURPOSES OF COVENANT, ESPECIALLY AS TO SANCTIONS AND THE CAUSES OF WAR
speechtext:
The idea is that machinery outside of the league is used, and in the solving of problems which may come up resort is had to old imperialistic methods rather than to the machinery of the league. In this morning's issue of the Montreal Gazette we see a very good example. It appears that Italy, having had a number of successful encounters with Ethiopian troops, is now saying to the French government that she is prepared to enter into negotiations with Ethiopia. However she is not making that statement to the league, nor is she using the machinery of the league. I maintain that if Italy and Ethiopia settle their differences outside the league by a mere juggling of territory we are sowing the seeds of another war. We cannot drive two horses in different harness. We must either work through the machinery set up by the league or resort to the old diplomatic balance of power which inevitably must lead to war.
Summing up, we take the attitude that if the League of Nations is to be used to maintain the status quo; if it is to be used so that the major nations, who have eaten their full in the race for colonies, may use the league to prevent the growth of other nations and to prevent economic expansion, and if it is to be used merely as a machine to enable those who have to keep what they have, we do not feel that such a league can be a satisfactory agency for peace. We maintain that if the League of Nations is used for what we believe it can be used, namely, an instrument of collective action, guaranteeing collective security and giving collective peace, if it is prepared to set up the machinery necessary to bring about revisions and readjustments in the international field, and if it is prepared to become a tribunal to which nations may go to air their grievances, it can, and I believe will, bceome a great power and a great force in the maintenance of world peace.
My submission is that no nation in the world has a greater responsibility or opportunity to that end than has Canada. We have no desire for colonies and no imperialistic dreams. We have no neighbours of whom we are afraid. Our relationship with our neighbours to the south stands a monument to peace and good will, and I suggest we are in a first class position to set up machinery

League of Nations-Mr. Marshall
which would give moral leadership to the nations of the world to the end that men of all races, colour and speech ultimately may come to sit in the parliament of man and the federation of the world.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak to this resolution I do so with a certain amount of trepidation. As a new member may I express to you, sir, and to the older members of this house- older not so much in point of age but in length of service-our appreciation of the courtesy and kindly tolerance which has been extended to us as a group of social crediters on account of the fact that we are new to this particular sphere.
The resolution before us is rather a long one, and it is not my purpose to discuss it in its entirety. I think it can be summed up in four words:	We want international
peace. I believe it is true, sir, that in the multiplicity of words there is much confusion, and in my own mind at least-I do not know whether in the mind of other members of the house-there is a certain amount of confusion as to exactly what this resolution means and exactly what it asks. I believe, too, that on account of conditions as they exist in Europe to-day it perhaps might be better if a resolution of this nature were not brought up for discussion.
Going back into the record of the proceedings of this house I find that discussions of international peace have taken place almost yearly since the great war ended in 1918. The hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Miss Maophail) has been most persistent in her demands for action by Canada in the cause of international peace, and she is to be commended for her action in that regard. I believe it is the duty of every red-blooded Canadian to seek every possible avenue which might lead to a solution of this problem When the war ended in 1918 we said that never again would we permit nations to bring such another catastrophe upon the world. We meant eveiy word we said in those days, and yet in spite of that we find the nations today flying at each other's throats. They have forgotten the expression "peace, perfect peace."
At the close of the war the League of Nations was set up, and it had two great aims: first, to preserve peace and to seek a peaceful settlement of international disputes,

and second, to organize in the most varied spheres the cooperation of peoples with a view to the material and moral welfare of humanity. These were very excellent aims, but I fear that to a great extent we have lost sight of that first aim, the preservation of peace.
To find out exactly what some of our leaders in this parliament have said and thought in regard to international peace I went back over the record of Hansard, and I find that the opinions expressed are very divergent indeed. They do not throw any new light on an old subject. Here are some opinions which were expressed on March 26, 1928. The present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), speaking on the subject of international peace, used these significant words:
This government and this parliament have identified themselves in a very real and immediate way with the League of Nations.
Everything we do in connection with the League of Nations we are doing along lines that are promoting this very objective-international peace.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), on a subsequent occasion, used these striking words:
There can be no educated public opinion so long as the machinery of parliaments is utilized for the purpose of providing armaments with which man may go to war.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) in 1930 used these words:
The old system has failed and a new structure is being built-
Those are very significant words indeed today. He continued:
-I hope on a basis of justice and solidarity. The League of Nations is no longer an idea; it has become a reality and its strength is continuously increasing.
Then we have the member for East Kootenay (Mr. Stevens) saying this:
You will never bring about peace by philosophical dissertations. There is only one method I know of and that is by promoting the principles of the Prince of Peace.
These, sir, are significant words, non-committal it is true, and general in their scope. Let us turn to some other comments. Let me read one which was made by the member for Broadview (Mr. Church). Commenting on an article written by George Bernard Shaw, the hon. member said:
Now let us see what Bernard Shaw has to say in regard' to this wonderful mock parliament known as the League of Nations, which is doing more to create strife than any other agency I know of. In my opinion they should change the name from League of Nations to League of Humbug, because that is all it is.

League oj Nations-Mr. Marshall
Then he goes on to quote the words of Bernard Shaw, who, I am sure you will agree with me, Mr. Speaker, is a man of thought, a master of English, and a moulder of public opinion. Bernard Shaw said:
Roughly and generally it is a fact that the pacifist oratory at the assembly is Christmas card platitude at best and humbug at worst. The permanent departments of the league have to fight hard to defeat the frequent attempts to sabotage it by the big powers through their deciduous members.
There you have, I think, the two schools of thought, one leaning towards the idea that the league is a successful institution, and the other suggesting that it has in a measure failed in its purpose, the purpose for which it was brought into being. Those who have criticized the League of Nations, it must be admitted, have had courage and daring. They may possibly be branded as men of warped intelligence, but notwithstanding that we ourselves in our hearts can criticize some of the actions of the league. No one will deny that the aim of the league, namely, the abolition of war, is a very worthy one indeed; but its sphere of activity has been so greatly widened that the primary aim, the abolition of war, has been lost sight of.
War is an inevitable result of the present financial system. I emphasize that with all the power at my command: war is an inevitable result of the present financial system. It has been said that war is economic peace and conversely peace is economic war. In peace nations enter into competition with one another for foreign markets in which to dispose of their surplus goods. I do not thinlj that anyone will gainsay that fact, and that invariably leads in practice to war. When there is war goods are destroyed almost as quickly as they come into existence; people are in possession of plenty of money and we have an all round stimulation of business; in other words, we have economic security. Some suggest that we should abolish entirely the manufacture of war materials. I heartily agree with that; and I think we are all agreed that the main reason for the boom which Great Britain and other nations are experiencing at the present time is the manufacture of war materials. But the question arises then: If you ban the manufacture of war materials what are you going to do with the unemployed? You will immediately throw people out of work; you will swell the ranks of the unemployed, and your problem is accentuated.
What is the solution of the problem? I think the solution lies in endeavouring to
bring to the consumer more than he is obtaining at present. Make your people happy and contented by giving them all they want to eat, all the clothes they can wear and decent homes to live in, and you will banish the incentive to go to war. The problem of peace is one that lies within our own border, and it lies in the realm of finance. I cannot stress that too strongly. Give the consumers of this country or any other country for that matter the necessary purchasing power to buy goods as produced and you will solve this problem of war.
Let me say this in conclusion. While I sympathize with the aim of this resolution, yet in a measure I am opposed to the means of attaining the end it sets forth. I wish to make a statement on behalf of this group with which I have the honour to be associated. We are opposed to war, but we are convinced that its prevention does not lie in its prohibition but rather in a removal of the causes that make war inevitable. The chief of these causes is the drive for foreign markets, and the reason for this struggle for markets is the present financial system, which makes it impossible for any nation to distribute its wealth amongst its own people. Until this fundamental cause is removed all talk of permanent peace is not only idle but misleading. Attempts to prohibit war without removing its causes must aggravate the disease. Prohibitions by sanctions may postpone war but will inevitably cause offensive alliances, thus in the end enlarging the scope of war.
Recognizing that we are a small nation, we realize that our only hope of securing lasting peace lies in cooperating with the English speaking nations of the world who alone have preserved the political freedom necessary to bring about economic reforms by constitutional methods. We are unalterably opposed to war except in defence of our political freedom.

Although the mover of the resolution (Mr. Douglas) is a member of our own group, perhaps I might be permitted to express my appreciation of the comprehensive and dignified manner in which he has dealt with this subject. With regard to the speech to which we have just listened, we are heartily agreed that the only real way to prevent war is to remove the causes that make for war. But we have to face a world in which Canada is not a self-contained country but is inevitably brought into relations with otner countries. We are to-day dealing with other countries. Under almost any circumstances that might be imagined, Canada would be dealing with other countries, and

674	COMMONS
League of Nations-Mr. Woodsworth
under these conditions when hostilities break out we simply have to face the issue. And it is in order that we may the more intelligently face that issue that the resolution is introduced to-day.
Before considering the resolution in detail, I should like to take this opportunity to call attention to a report of a speech 'by the Italian consul, Luigi Petrucci, given before the Italian chamber of commerce yesterday in Montreal. It seems to me that this is a most improper speech and a very dangerous one. After criticizing very severely the League of Nations of which we are a member, and which league has condemned the action of Italy, he goes on to say-I will quote only part of the article which appears in the first column of page 2 of this morning's Montreal Gazette:
I cannot refrain from expressing my sorrow because Canada is applying sanctions against Italy, sanctions which are dangerous because they can bring another world war and which have destroyed the Italo-Canadian trade, which only a few months ago the two countries were trying to improve by means of a new commercial convention.
These sanctions cannot stop the Italian enterprise in East Africa. Other effects of sanctions are that they will create a great wall between nations and will make economic liberalism even more unrealizable and utopian. The covenant will become more and more difficult to apply and economic wars between nations will become the rule.	_	.
Italy refuses to admit the judgment taken by the League of Nations against her as illegal and iniquitous, and will stand with all her strength to oppose the effects of sanctions.
That is a challenge to Canada, and a challenge to the league, uttered by one who enjoys special privileges and special immunities in this country. I submit that it is ample ground for asking for his withdrawal from this country as the consul of Italy. May I further say that this is not the first time that we have had trouble with this particular consul. Members will remember something of this kind about a year ago, if I recall aright. Further, I remember last year a deputation of Italian citizens waiting upon me here in Ottawa, they having come from Montreal to make certain charges against the consul. They chimed that with his connivance there was being built up a secret fascist organization called the nationalist organization for the repression of anti-fascism. They charged that the officials of this organization were paid by the Italian government notwithstanding that they were British subjects 'by naturalization. They charged that the consul exercised a great deal of intimidation over Canadian citizens; that, naturally, Canadian citizens had to go to the consul for a
[Mr. Woodsworth.1
good many things relating to their homeland -certificates of birth and so on; that when they did so the accommodation was refused them unless they joined the fascist organization, and further that threats were made, not merely of bodily harm to Canadian citizens here but also to relatives of Canadian citizens who were still in Italy. There was shown to me a photostat of what purported to be an oath which was being administered by the consul to Canadian citizens. This ran as follows:
In the name of God and Italy I swear to execute the orders of II Duce and to serve with all my strength and if necessary with my blood the cause of the fascist revolution.
I am not prepared, obviously, as a private citizen to make investigation as to how far these charges are justified. I turned over the memorandum, which was submitted to me by a lawyer of Montreal who appeared with the delegation, to the Department of External Affairs. I do not know whether any action has been taken, but I submit that these are serious charges and ought to be carefully investigated. I have not brought this matter to the attention of the house, but when such statements are made, as appeared in the Montreal Gazette to-day, it is high time that some action should be taken by the government.
Coming to the resolution, may I point out that in the past it has been extremely difficult to get a discussion of foreign affairs. I do not know why it is, but it has been the practice to bring in the estimates of the Department of External Affairs very near to the close of the session. I am glad to say that that practice has been modified this year, and we already have had before us some of these estimates. But year after year about the only opportunity the house has had of discussing foreign or external affairs has been on the estimates, and they have come in very late. Last year-I do not say it was done by design-they came in late one evening just at the close of the estimates of another department. One minister was not prepared to go on; a switch was made to the Department of External Affairs, and the estimates went through without even a single comment; in fact there was not even a reference to them-I suppose for that reason-in Hansard. One result of this lack of discussion in parliament had been that our people generally have not been very much accustomed to discussing foreign affairs. Of course it is quite true that with us foreign affairs have more largely to do with our relations with the United States, but notwith-

League of Nations-Mr. Woodsworth
standing that fact I think we all must recognize that in the last great war we were thrown into the struggle, and in all probability we may be thrown into another great struggle.

subtopic: FULFILMENT OF OBLIGATIONS AND PURPOSES OF COVENANT, ESPECIALLY AS TO SANCTIONS AND THE CAUSES OF WAR
speechtext:
That struggle led to the sacrifice of the lives of tens of thousands of our best young men and brought this country to a condition of bankruptcy or near bankruptcy. It is curious that although we participated in one great war and are in danger of being thrown into another, we take no very active part in actually discussing external affairs. I have expressed on several occasions the hope that the reports of the League of Nations delegates should be referred to the committee on industrial and international affairs. Almost anything that would stimulate an interest among Canadians in the matter of our external relationships ought to be welcomed. The Prime Minister the other day, discussing the estimates for his own department, referred in this house to the way in which external affaire were pressing in upon us in recent years. They are bound to do so, and yet any crisis that arises finds our people quite unprepared.
A few years ago Canada was a signatory of the so-called Kellogg pact, in which we definitely abandoned war as an instrument of national policy. Nearly all the leading nations of the world signed that pact, and yet none of us apparently has implemented it by any change in national policy. I urge that not only should we abandon war as an instrument of national policy but we should abandon it as a recognized means for settlement of international disputes. Such a settlement is not permanent. The organization with which I am connected stands opposed to war. In order to make very clear our position I would read a statement with respect to peace, published two years ago at our Winnipeg convention:
We recognize that modern war rises primarily from the clash of interests in a world economy based on competition, therefore the establishment of world peace depends on abolishing competition and on building a cooperative commonwealth.
I trust that hon. members will not accuse me of unduly dragging in party considerations We were thinking of much larger things than any Canadian party when we spoke of it. The statement proceeds:
The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation is ualterably opposed' to war. If the great capitalist powers drift into another war Canadian neutrality must be rigorously maintained whoever the belligerents may be. Canada must refuse to give military assistance to the League
of Nations as at present constituted. We stand for thorough reorganization of the league in order to make it an effective instrument of peace.
The last clause of the resolution before the house is as follows:
That unless and until there is a sincere acceptance and application of the above by the member-nations of the league, Canada will refuse to participate in any foreign war, no matter who the belligerents may be.
Personally I would go farther than that. The longer I live the more convinced I become that war settles nothing, that war is the greatest disaster that could come upon any nation. I am convinced of that. I do not care whether or not somebody dubs me pacifist, with all the rather opprobrious connotations of that word; I think it is the only sane and safe policy in the world to-day. I have a good deal of respect for Mr. George Lansbury who, speaking of his resignation as leader of the Labour party in Great Britain, made this statement:
It is impossible for me to believe anything good can come out of mass murder, whether this is carried out by order of a league of nations or by a single nation. Evil cannot be swept out of our lives by evil; the spirit of war cannot be destroyed by more war.
I want to adopt that statement as my own, so there may be no doubt in the mind of any hon. member as to where I stand.
We come to the policies of our country, and as yet, unfortunately in my judgment, this country, like a good many other countries is still relying more or less upon armaments as a last resort. I suggest that an isolationist position cannot be successfully maintained' in the world to-day. Things may come to such a pass, if we are about to be dragged into a war and there may be no other policy open to us. We may be forced to adopt an isolationist policy and refuse to be dragged in. But it should be remembered that to-day the world is becoming more or less integrated industrially, financially and socially. We cannot stay out by ourselves. As long as we are in the world neighbourhood we have to deal with the people whom we meet in that neighbourhood. So we ought to recognize that the League of Nations, in so far as it is an association of nations seeking to promote peace, ought to be supported.
We are also of course a member of the British empire. Two years ago I had the opportunity to attend, as a delegate, the Canadian Institute of International Affairs, which met at Toronto in association with the Royal Institute of International Affairs, which has headquarters at Chatham House. Viscount
676	COMMONS
League of Nations-Mr. Woodsworth
Cecil led the British delegation, which included Liberals, Conservatives and Labour men. We discussed the question as to what would happen if, perchance, the interests of Great Britain and the League of Nations should not be identical, which should claim our loyalty. Possibly the answer to that question was evaded, because there were certain differences of opinion, but the conclusions finally adopted were to the effect that we could not possibly see that the interests of Great Britain could be divergent from the interests of the league itself. So I do not think we need discuss our special obligations to the British empire; they ought to be identical with those we owe the league.
I frankly confess, Mr. Speaker, that the league as now constituted is a very imperfect instrument for maintaining world peace. For some years I declined to join the League of Nations Society, just for that reason. At that time the league seemed to me essentially a league of victors. For a time the situation improved. Now the United States is still out; Germany came in and went out; and Japan is out. The entry of the U.SjS.R. into the league, meant a distinct advance but still it is essentially only a partial league of nations.
Further than that, national sovereignty is still maintained. I know every nation is jealous of what it claims to be its own final right to decide things, but just as within our national life smaller groups have given up their voices in the presence of the larger groups, so it seems to me we ultimately must come to the place where we will be willing to sacrifice for the common good what we have hitherto claimed to be our national sovereignty. I think we will have to come to that. To-day two people come to the court; they ask the court to make a decision, and then they loyally accept the decision that is made. As nations we refuse to do that. In the first place we all maintain our armaments, and a number of nations persist in carrying on a line of independent action. Just recently, for example, Great Britain held some naval manoeuvres in the Mediterranean, taking independent action at the very time when it would seem that every move should have been taken through the league.
I will admit, too, that to a large extent the league to-day is dominated by the great powers. Several years ago it was largely dominated by France. To-day I think the predominate influence is that of Great Britain. The great empires have their own ends to serve. I think that can be said without particularly casting reflections upon them as empires. They have their own ends to serve;

they are not impartial judges. In my judgment there is a very great danger that the league may be made a kind of smoke screen behind which imperialist aims and ambitions may be carried forward. I am not ashamed of being a Britisher, but I unite with a great many Britishers living in Great Britain in denouncing imperialism as we know it in modern days, and imperialism is none the less to be denounced because it is British imperialism. We denounce German imperialism and French imperialism and Japanese imperialism, and I cannot exclude British imperialism. 1 do not think Great Britain had been worse than most empires, but as we look back through history and see the processes and developments that have taken place we must admit that our British empire has been built up by methods none of us to-day would care to justify.
Now let me say a few words with regard to sanctions. I think we may distinguish between economic sanctions and military sanctions. I know there is a danger that economic sanctions may provoke an enemy in a desperate position to reprisals, perhaps even to the declaration of war. In the case of Italy I cannot but think that a declaration of that kind on our proposal to extend sanctions was a good deal of a bluff. However, there is that possibility. As the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) suggested in moving the resolution, however, there is also the danger that unless we do exercise economic sanctions we may very easily provoke war. There is danger in every direction, but if we were only sincere and thorough-going in our exercise of sanctions it seems to me we would not have to face war. Take this question of oil. I do not know the ins and outs of the handling of oil. I do know Great Britain is said to have a very considerable number of shares in the Anglo-Persian Oil Corporation. I know something of the part that oil has played in the past, and it may be that there has been pressure on the British government from the oil companies. I do not know. A few weeks ago it seemed as if the United States, despite the difficulty of the president taking action along this line, might possibly have joined with other nations in bringing oil sanctions into effect. But if sanctions are to be applied, they must be made effective, and all nations must be willing to do their share. I am glad to think that at last we have come to the point of recognizing the desirability of not allowing war materials to pass into the hands of the aggressor. I think it is two years since I brought in a resolution in regard to nickel, urging that we express our willing-

League of Nations-Mr. Woodsworth
ness to cooperate with the League of Nations in seeing that no nickel found its way into war materials. That resolution was not adopted by this house. Here is an extract from a stock market publication, issued a little less than a year ago; it is given in the League of Nations Society in Canada monthly news sheet:
Current demands for nickel are running at a record making rate, moving ahead with the added force of peace time requirements. In addition, there has been little let up by the purchases by many nations of armaments and this has meant in one way or another the buying of nickel. Neaidy all major powers are increasing substantially their naval and military appropriations. These and other factors seem to promise a rising curve of nickel consumption, production and earnings.
I cannot see that we as a nation can escape responsibility for having continued to send abroad nickel that has been finding its way into the making of war materials. Here is a recent Canadian Press dispatch which appeared on the regular financial page dated at Ottawa, November 20, with regard to nickel:
The Dominion Bureau of Statistics disclosed, Tuesday, that Italy, apparently racing to get under the League of Nations' sanctions wire, imported from 'Canada almost twice as much fine nickel in October as it did during all last year, increasing its total imports from Canada 119 per cent, compared' with October, 1934.
And the dispatch goes on to speak of the greatly increased production and shipment of copper. I am glad that we have stopped the exportation of nickel-at least I hope we have. At Brockville the other day a railway employee pointed across the railway yards to a car which he said was loaded with nickel and which was being stopped in transit. That is at least some indication that perhaps action is being taken. But I submit that we should have taken action two years ago, and very drastic action, even before we formally consented to join in these sanctions.
The purpose of the resolution is to point out that sanctions in themselves are not enough. We say that we should remain loyal to the terms of the covenant. That may be, but may I point out that there are other clauses in the covenant besides 10 and 16. Take the first clause in article 8:
The members of the league recognize that the maintenance of peace requires the reduction of national armaments to the lowest point consistent with national safety and the enforcement by common action of international obligations.
Have the countries of the world actually disarmed? Instead of that they have been arming, and now we are told that Great Rritain is giving up the idea that there will
not be a war within ten years; her leading statesmen are saying that war will almost inevitably come inside of four years, and so a greater armament campaign is being proposed. We asked Germany to disarm, and Germany disarmed under the express condition that the other nations would do the same. The other nations did not carry out their solemn obligations to Germany, with the result that an almost desperate German people developed fascism. We have not carried out our obligations under section 8 of the covenant.
Then there is section 19, which I think is not quite so familiar to some of our people. It is very short:
The assembly may from time to time advise the reconsideration by members of the league of treaties which have become inapplicable and the consideration of international' conditions whose continuance might endanger the peace of the world.
There is no doubt that a great many treaties that exist are not applicable to-day. There is no doubt in my mind that the Versailles treaty is not a just treaty. In many ways it ought to be revised. Under pressure from Germany certain clauses have been slightly revised. We are willing to concede now that Germany was not wholly responsible for the war. The provisions with regard to reparation payments have become in effect dead letters, but we have not made those general revisions that seem to be justified if the peace of the world is to be preserved. I feel very strongly that some responsible body must undertake to get at the causes of war, the causes of friction. That was one of the purposes for which the league was set up. A few weeks ago there was a discussion of the league policy carried on under the auspices of the League of Nations Society in Canada. Comments were sent in from various members of the society, and a number of them were published in the organ of the society. Among others I find this:
Her (the Canadian) representatives have two distinct questions to answer for her people, before they can properly take or support action at Geneva. One is: what can she do through her own government, and in cooperation with other nations, to satisfy the claims and desires of Italy that are just and genuinely in accord with civilized life, and thus prevent war?_______If war is the alternative, the Canadian people should be allowed to choose between a war, and its consequences near and far, and a reorganization of her economic and social life....
Until some powerful effort has been made by Canada or someone else to attack the causes of war, and to remove them by paying a price
678	COMMONS
League oj Nations-Mr. Woodsworth
which however great cannot be as great as war itself, Canada should not become involved in any system of sanctions which under those circumstances would not be sanction-that is the force of equitable authority

at all, but would simply be the old-fashioned private war used by a stronger group to assert its will.
Thus we are forced to recognize the danger of sanctions unaccompanied by other action. Sanctions in themselves might simply maintain the status quo, which might prevent a just solution of existing problems. Lord Lothian put this matter very clearly in a speech delivered on September 28 of last year:
We have allowed it (the league) to become an instrument not for settling grievances but for perpetuating a status quo which is every year becoming more difficult to justify.
A few days later Sir Herbert Samuel put it this way:
The League of Nations must become something more than a mere defender of the status quo.
May I quote once more from Lord Lothian in a speech delivered on September 18 of last year:
Italy has a case against us and the league -a much better case than she has against Abyssinia. In the last century there was practically free migration all over the world, and in substance free trade in goods, foodstuffs and capital. To-day the nations are living in watertight compartments, with no migration and no freedom of trade, with the result that many of them have got into such tremendous population and economic difficulties that they have resorted to dictatorship to maintain order at home, and most of them are adding to their armaments in order to try to solve their internal problems by action in a foreign field.
In summing up my position I believe I could do no better than quote the observations of Mr. Eseott Reid in a statement before the National Council of the League of Nations Society in November:
An effective collective system means not only the restraint of the aggresor but also disarmament, international instead of imperial control of colonies, and effective machinery to deal with treaty revision and the problems of markets, migration and raw materials. The crisis which presents itself to-day gives us an opportunity to build the foundations and perhaps some of the framework of such a system. If we seize that opportunity we shall greatly diminish the prospects of war. If we fail to seize it, war will not be far off.
I know it is very difficult for most of us to come to anything like a satisfactory conclusion in connection with the Italo-Ethiopian tangle. I should like to express my personal sympathies for Ethiopia. I cannot see how possibly we could too strongly condemn Italy's action. At the same time I am conscious that other nations have sinned in much the
Mr. Woodsworth.]
same way as has Italy. I have before me a volume published several years ago by the late John S. Ewart, entitled Canada and British Wars. Could anyone read a document such as this without realizing that in nearly all disputes of recent time Great Britain has been at fault as have other empires, in the wars of imperial expansion. Undoubtedly the British empire has been built up by methods not greatly dissimilar from those now being used by Italy and Japan. I think of India, of Egypt from 1882 to 1895, of the Venezuela boundary dispute of 1895-6, of Persia in 1896, of South Africa in 1895 and through to 1902, of the Anglo-Japanese alliance of 1902, of our relationships with France, 1898-1914; of the Moroccan crisis, 1905-6, of the Anglo-Russian relationships, 1906-7; of the triple entente 1907, and of all the difficulties we had in Morocco and Persia and the Balkans; of British action in China, and so on.
Hon. members of my own generation will recall the difficulties which were experienced in connection with these matters. One cannot go back over the history of modem imperialism without realizing that there is much to be deplored. At the same time that does not mean that we can condone what Italy is now doing, but it does mean that we must frankly recognize our responsibility in the matter. I do not often feel like quoting Mr. Amery, but I should like to read a statement he made a few months ago. Hon. members are aware that he was former dominions and colonial secretary. He said:
There is something rather humorous in a gorged and satiated lion reproving a hungry young tiger, saying it sympathizes with him, but his appetite must be satisfied in accordance with the rules of the vegetarian society, of which the lion has been the last joining member.
There is a great deal in that statement. Along similar lines Sir Stafford Cripps made this statement at the Brighton Labour party conference:
It is argued that Mussolini will be crushed. He will not. In all probability he will drive a satisfactory bargain with his fellow members of the international burglars union momentarily termed policemen.

League oj Nations-Miss Macphail
Miss AGNES C. MACPHAIL (Grey-Bruce): Mr. Speaker, I am sure the resolution of the hon. member for Weybum (Mr. Douglas) is of interest to all hon. members. Undoubtedly a very strong opinion in Canada against Canadian participation in European wars was shown during the last campaign, when parties and groups, either through conviction or because of their desire to say things which were pleasant to the ears of the electors, took the same stand on this question. Every party or group whose campaign literature reached me, or whose speeches I read in the press, stood against Canadian participation in European war, until wre had consulted the people through a plebiscite or something of the sort. Then if people decided that they wanted to go to war, then they would go to war. I believe the party in power took the stand that Canada would not participate in any European war until the matter had been submitted to parliament, which in practice would mean submission to the Liberal party.
The feeling on this matter of a great many people is one of confusion and uncertainty. I find myself troubled by the common ground taken by the imperialists and the enthusiasts for the league on the matter of sanctions. It is the first occasion of which I am aware that they have taken the same ground, and they seem to be about equally enthusiastic though I am quite sure, for different reasons.
The whole question of sanctions brought the matter of participation in European war clearly before us, and any thinking person has to come to some conclusion or other in regard to it.
For many years I have been exceedingly enthusiastic about the league and have been hopeful that it was the organization in the world which was going to do the most to remove the causes of war. I have always been more interested in removing causes than in the maintenance of peace by force. Peace maintained by force, whether the force be called sanctions or by some other name, is a precarious peace. In my view the only peace which can be lasting is one which arises as the natural consequence of the removal of the causes of war. My undimmed enthusiasm for the League of Nations lasted until the disarmament conference. My faith in British sincerity in maintaining world peace through the action of the league lasted until the disarmament conference, but I say to this house quite frankly that I have never been as enthusiastic on either point since the failure of the disarmament conference. I feel that at that time Canada did not take as strong a stand as she might have done. She took just a nominal stand, and did not put up the
fight at the conference that I would have wished to see. I was not pleased with the attitude of Great Britain at that time. I did feel then, and I have felt since, and do feel now that we lost a tremendous opportunity at that time, and it is one that may not recur. It may after another blood bath, or it may never.
In reading over the resolution I feel myself in harmony with most of the statements made therein-it is rather too long to read again- but I want to take some little time to say that I feel the greatest need of Canada and all the other countries which are sincerely anxious for world peace is the pressing for the application of article 19 of the covenant. I think that if we are only going to go on invoking sanctions, we are wielding a big stick which will eventually not be successful. It may now be successful, but the time will come when the group of nations which "have not" will become as strong, by combinations, as the group of nations which "have," and when that time comes sanctions will not be effective. So I think if we are going to remain in the league we ought as a country to take the wrork of the league very seriously. We ought first to have a Department of External Affairs that is not headed by the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), speaking of this matter the other evening said, and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) agreed with him, that he would have to know what went on in that department anyway, and with that I agree; still if that department were headed by a person who specialized in international matters, his consultation with the Prime Minister would make it a stronger department than it could possibly be when headed by an altogether overworked man, as the Prime Minister of Canada must be. So I think we should have a Department of External Affairs with a minister at its head apart from the Prime Minister.
I believe, too, that we should raise the status of our representative at Geneva. I believe that we ought to take the road to peace definitely. But what we have been doing, and everybody in this house knows it, is trying to take both roads-peace and war-at once. We have not been spending much money on peace or on the Department of External Affairs or on our office in Geneva. We have not even made a place on the agenda of the House of Commons for a report of the delegates when they come back from Geneva. We thought what they did at the league of so little consequence that we did not even provide on the agenda a place for

League oj Nations-Miss Macphail
their report when the delegates returned, so that they could make clear to the house what went on there and what the stand of Canada was. And we should send to the league only people who are members of parliament, either of this house or of the upper house. It is simply ridiculous to send people who are not members of either house. It has been a method of rewarding people who have been kind to the party in power or some such thing. It has no meaning so far as the peace work is concerned.
So if Canada is going to stay in the league I would like to see her seriously undertake the work because nominal support is likely to draw us into sanctions and into war, without our ever having used the league as an instrument for the preservation of peace. I think we have come to the place where we must decide what we are going to do, whether we are going to stay in the league and be active members of it, or not stay in at all.
I hear a good many people talking about the happy results that would come from an English speaking alliance. May I say that I think a great deal of danger lies in that direction unless we clearly recognize the differences in interest and the different areas of the earth which constitute the first interest of the great English speaking nations. It is true that Britain and the United States have very much in common. There is no quarrelling about frontiers; there is no wrangling over spheres of influence or over the expansion of their empires. In fact, they are both contracting and are getting out from under the weight of their imperial interests by gradually, and sometimes rapidly, giving self-government to their dependencies. The Philippines would serve as an example in the American sphere, and the growing power of the dominions and of India in the British sphere. As far as we have gone now, Great Britain and America have a similar outlook on world politics. Then they have this other thing, which is greater than all; they have a common tradition, and they have a common language. But we are apt, when we have come to see that all this is true, to jump to the conclusion that their interests are therefore identical. May I take a moment to point out that their interests are not identical; their most immediate and pressing problems are not the same, and if we recognize that fact it will save us future disappointment. Let me quote a paragraph from Walter Lippmann on this point. He says:
American isolation is one of the optical illusions of the present era. American policy is conditioned by its vital interests just as is
[Miss Maephail.l
British policy. Thus America is isolationist as to continental Europe, but it has never been and is not now isolationist in the region of the Caribbean or the Pacific ocean. The British ardour for the league is a reflection of British interest in British security; the lack of British ardour for the collective system in the Far East is a reflection of a greater concern with European security.	_
He goes on to say about his own country:
So it is with us. President Harding, who was elected in 1920 as a result of a rebellion against the league, signed a whole series of treaties in 1922 which applied the league's principles to the Orient. In 1931 Secretary Stimson stood forth as the protagonist of league principles and Sir John Simon did not.
I think that is true, and I think it is an explanation of why Great Britain was not as much interested in invoking certain articles in the league covenant in relation to Japanese aggression in Manchuria as was the United States, and of why Great Britain is much more interested in invoking certain articles of the covenant in relation to Italy's aggression in Ethiopia than the United States is, and, in fact, than we are. Whether we like to admit it or not, and I for one quite frankly admit it, Canadians are North Americans. We have a divided interest. While sentimentally and patriotically we are bound closely to Great Britain, economically and geographically we are bound to the North American continent. So that we find it difficult-at least I find it difficult, and I believe a great many other Canadians do-to be as enthusiastic about" invoking sanctions in Europe at the moment as Britishers are. I find myself irritated by the continued animosity of Europeans; I find myself remote from these continual quarrels, and I believe we all do-which is only another way of saying that we live on the North American continent. I venture to say that if the English channel were as wide as the Atlantic, Great Britain's reaction to European problems would quite likely be exactly ours. I feel therefore that while doing everything we can to foster good will and understanding among English speaking nations, we ought to recognize the differences that exist. If we did we should not be so much disappointed over the lack of British interest in the far east and the lack of American interest in continental Europe. For it simply means that their greatest concern is respectively in that area in which their first interest lies.
When I was in the United States shortly before this house opened I heard some Oxford students discussing these questions-and very able young men they were. In my opinion they were stressing unduly this question of friendship between English speaking

League of Nations-Miss Macphail
peoples; I could not help feeling that they were not recognizing the differences that actually exist. They were more or less chiding the United States for not being as much interested in the European problem as Great Britain was, when it was evident to anyone looking at a map of the world that the United States would not have the same interest. I do not think their visit did any good; I do not think it helped the very thing they came to promote, whereas if they had recognized that each was loyal to the sphere of its first interest they would have accomplished more.
I have always been extremely opposed to war and I am still; but I am not so much interested in whether Canadian boys die in one kind of war as distinguished from another as I am in keeping them from dying in any sort of war. I cannot therefore work up very much enthusiasm about military sanctions. What I want to prevent is war; and in the last two or three years we have found the nations of the world apparently seeking peace in several ways, the three most outstanding being collective security and at the same time, and running parallel, a race in armaments, simultaneously with pacts outside the league, until some writer-I forget who it was -said there was a bad epidemic of pacto-mania. Now these three methods pursued at the same time do not make sense. I can understand reliance on an armament race and on pacts, but I cannot understand collective security with a race in armaments and at the same time pacts outside the league.
In this house over a long period of years I have noticed the same thing-fear of trying new peace methods. The house apparently has been afraid to abandon the old military methods but has run along timidly with a short step in the direction of peace and a long step on the military road. We have almost forgotten the ideas that emerged from the war. One of the sentences of Woodrow Wilson we ought always to remember; it is: that peace must be peace without victory, for only peace between equals can last. Well, it was not peace without victory and certainly it was not peace between equals; and instead of seeking to make it peace between equals, as time went on, there was a disposition on the part of the league to defend the status quo in Europe. And it is the invoking of sanctions in defence of the status quo that I fear more than anything else.
It is true that the League of Nations has worked out-I am happy about this-the technique of cooperation through conference, and by doing so it has been able to make a very considerable contribution to all the nations and to our common life, which is the
community of the world. It is true too that in these conferences many errors have been made from time to time; but it is also true that invariably when errors have been made the nations have been called together again in conference and some at any rate of the errors have been rectified. But though the league has worked out the technique of cooperation through conference, it has never attempted to invoke article 19 of the covenant. This article was read by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) but I should like to read it again, because it is that part of the covenant which we shall all have to learn thoroughly in the future:
The assembly may from time to time advise the reconsideration by members of the league of treaties which have become inapplicable and the consideration of international conditions whose continuance might endanger the peace of the world.
I think t'he task of the league now is to invoke article 19; and while I certainly have no sympathy with Italy, I do believe that in the long run the invoking of that article is infinitely more important than the whole question of sanctions. In my opinion the future of the league will depend upon its ability to invoke article 19 and to settle perplexing economic and racial problems through the method of cooperation, because it is more and more becoming realized that all nations should have access to raw materials and to areas and to markets. I feel that Sir Samuel Hoare will be remembered, because he made a strong speech on this subject, long after the Hoare-Laval-misnamed-peace .proposal is forgotten, because in emphasizing the need of nations having access to raw materials and areas and markets he did strike the thing that is vital. It is true that there are other considerations. The carving up of Europe, the taking away of the hinterland of countries that cannot very well get along as they are now constituted, the dividing of people who should be one racially and culturally, are also grievances that are likely to lead to war. Yet I think that the economic cause is the greatest, and that we need as a League of Nations and as a country that is a member of the League of Nations very seriously to take up the question of remedying these grievances rather than to seek to keep things as they are 'by using sanctions in defence of the status quo.
While it is true that the principle of graduated responsibility in relation to sanctions has been recognized, I think it has not been sufficiently realized that those who are most involved need to take the initiative and to assume the greatest responsibility in the in-
